name: Four-in-hand knot

lead: The four-in-hand is one of the simplest ways to tie a necktie. It produces a narrow, elongated, slightly asymmetric knot that sits neatly at the collar and is often chosen for a polished but unfussy look.

It helps appearance through tailoring: a slimmer knot balances narrow ties and lapels and avoids the bulk of larger knots. Style writers and forum users describe it as versatile, but no research has tested its effect on how a person is perceived.

paras: The wide end is crossed over the narrow end, wrapped around it, brought across the front and tucked through the loop at the top, then snugged up to the collar. Because it is asymmetric, a slight natural slant is part of the look. Practitioners pair it with button-down and spread collars and with slim or textured ties.

There are no health risks. The knot can look too small on very wide ties or with wide-spread collars, and asymmetry is intentional, so users who want a symmetrical knot choose a half-Windsor or Windsor.

angle.text: The knot changes how the neckline of a shirt and jacket looks. Its narrow shape suits slim ties and button-down collars, and its asymmetry gives a deliberately casual finish.

lead: The four-in-hand knot is a method of tying a necktie that yields a narrow, notably asymmetric triangle of fabric at the collar [1]. It is also known as the simple, schoolboy or cravat knot, and as the bucket knot in the UK [1]. For people dressing to look sharper, it is a standard everyday knot.

Wikipedia describes the process as crossing the broad end in front of the narrow end, wrapping behind, passing horizontally across the front and tucking through the top before sliding it up to the collar [1]. Compared with it, the half-Windsor is more symmetric and slightly broader, and the Windsor is more symmetric and substantially bulkier [1].

Its origin is commonly linked to the Four-in-Hand Club of London, whose members are said to have worn this neckwear, though carriage-driver explanations also exist [1][2]. It is one of three necktie knots prescribed for US Army and Navy uniforms [1].
infobox: Simple knot, schoolboy knot, bucket knot (UK) [1]

paras: The four-in-hand is notably asymmetric and narrow [1]. Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, describes it as formed by wrapping the wide end around the narrow end two or three times before tucking it through the loop [2]. Style writers recommend it for narrow ties, button-down collars and textured fabrics, though these recommendations are not covered in Wikipedia's article.

The name is commonly traced to the Four-in-Hand Club in London, whose members wore this neckwear, which made it fashionable [1]. Other accounts say carriage drivers used a similar knot to secure scarves or reins, and Grokipedia cites Clifford Ashley's Ashley Book of Knots (1944) on the knot's horsy background [2]. The same knot used as a rope hitch is called the buntline hitch, used by sailors during the Age of Sail [1].
A variant, the Onassis knot, wraps the long end over the finished knot and was popularised briefly by Aristotle Onassis [1].
On fashion forums such as T Nation, men discuss dressing fundamentals, building a wardrobe around a few reliable pieces and presenting in a traditional business manner [3][4].
